paper.title_en: Fast X-ray Transients as Premature-Dissipated Gamma-Ray Bursts with Magnetic-Dominated Jets
paper.abstract_en: Fast X-ray transients (FXTs) are extragalactic X-ray flashes with little or no accompanying $γ$-ray emission. We propose that FXTs and classical gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) share a common origin in Poynting-flux-dominated jets powered by the Blandford--Znajek mechanism. In this picture, FXTs arise when the kink instability triggers premature dissipation at small radii ($\sim 10^{11}$~cm), yielding low Lorentz factors ($Γ\lesssim 50$) and high compactness ($\ell' \gg 1$) that thermalize the emission into the soft X-ray band. When the kink criterion is not met, the jet accelerates to ultra-relativistic velocities ($Γ> 100$) and dissipates at larger radii ($\sim 10^{15}$~cm) as a standard GRB. This scenario can naturally explain the observed thermal spectra, low $E_{\rm peak}$, supernova associations, jet-break absence, and day-scale afterglow delays across five well-studied FXTs. EP240801a is explained as a boundary event, where premature dissipation does not exhaust the full magnetic energy; the residual energy is further dissipated at a typical GRB radius, producing the observed $γ$-ray prompt emission with an $\sim 80$~s time lag. A key observational prediction is that FXTs may exhibit $e^+ e^-$ annihilation line features sweeping from a few MeV to hundreds of keV within $\sim 0.01$~s.
